usage: to go in to the company / office
회사에 takes 에 (destination), not 에서; this is the default partner phrase
제시간에 = at the appointed time; the everyday opposite is 지각하다 (be late)
to come in to work early
일찍 (early) pairs naturally; its opposite 늦게 출근하다 means come in late
to come into the office instead of working from home
재택근무 = working from home; shows 출근 = physically going IN, not just 'working'
examples: 저는 회사에 출근해요.
I go to work (to the company).
Plain daily statement; note 회사에 with 에, marking where you head TO
보통 아홉 시까지 출근해요.
I usually get to work by nine.
아홉 시까지 = 'by nine'; 까지 sets the deadline you must arrive within
몸이 너무 아파서 오늘은 출근 못 해요.
I'm so sick I can't come in to work today.
Negative-ability 못 해요 splits as 출근 못 해요, never 못 출근해요
nuance: 출근하다 is Sino-Korean 出勤 — 出 'go out' + 勤 'duty/diligence' — so literally 'go out to your duty', i.e. physically travel to your workplace and start your shift. Its exact opposite is 퇴근하다 (退勤, leave work). Do not confuse 출근하다 with plain 일하다 'to work': 출근하다 is the act of arriving/clocking in, while 일하다 is the doing of work itself — 회사에 출근해서 여덟 시간 일해요 (I go in and then work eight hours). Because it is a noun(출근) + 하다 verb, every form built off the 하다 part: dictionary 출근하다, 요-form 출근해요 (하 + 여 contracts to 해), past 출근했어요, formal 출근합니다. The English-speaker pitfall is twofold: first, the negative and impossible forms split the noun off — 출근 안 해요 and 출근 못 해요, never 안 출근해요; second, the place takes 에 (destination) not 에서, so 회사에 출근해요 is right and 회사에서 출근해요 (which would mean leaving from the company) is wrong.

structuredNuance.t: Physically travel to your workplace and start your shift. The act of arriving/clocking in, not the work itself.

Using 출근하다 for the general idea of 'working'. To go in is 출근하다; to actually do the work is 일하다.

usage: to leave work on time / clock out on time
제시간에 = on the dot; the dreaded opposite is 야근하다 (work overtime)
to leave work right on the dot (not a minute over)
칼 'knife' + 퇴근 = a sharp, exactly-on-time exit; very common casual slang
일찍 pairs naturally; opposite 늦게 퇴근하다 = leave late
to grab a drink after leaving work
the 하고 here means 'and then'; 한잔하다 = have a drink, the classic after-work plan
examples: 여섯 시에 퇴근해요.
I leave work at six.
Clock time of a one-moment event takes 에: 여섯 시에
오늘은 일이 많아서 늦게 퇴근해요.
There's a lot of work today, so I'm leaving late.
~아서 gives the reason; 늦게 = late (adverb)
우리 같이 퇴근할까요?
Shall we head out together?
~ㄹ까요? proposes; coworkers say this to walk out together
nuance: 퇴근하다 is Sino-Korean 退勤 — 退 'withdraw/retreat' + 勤 'duty' — literally 'withdraw from your duty', i.e. finish the workday and head home. It is the precise mirror of 출근하다 (出勤). Don't confuse it with 끝나다 'to end' or 쉬다 'to rest': 퇴근하다 specifically means YOU leave the workplace, whereas 일이 끝나다 means the work is finished and 쉬다 means to take a break. As a noun+하다 verb it conjugates entirely on 하다: 퇴근해요, 퇴근했어요, formal 퇴근합니다. The English-speaker pitfall is the same family of splits — the negative is 퇴근 안 해요 and the impossible form 퇴근 못 해요, never 안 퇴근해요. A second trap: English 'get off work' tempts learners to invent a particle, but 퇴근하다 takes no object at all; the time is enough — 여섯 시에 퇴근해요. Beware the very common slang 칼퇴근(하다), 'knife clock-out', meaning you leave at the exact end time without a second of overtime.

structuredNuance.t: Finish the workday and head home — YOU leave the workplace. Watch the very common slang 칼퇴근(하다), 'knife clock-out', meaning you leave at the exact end time without a second of overtime.

usage: the school takes 를/을 (object), NOT 에서 — 대학교를 졸업해요
성적으로 = 'with grades'; 으로 marks the manner/standing you finish in
~ㄴ 후에 = after; the past-modifier 졸업한 attaches to 후
to be on the verge of graduating
앞두다 = to have something just ahead; 졸업을 앞둔 학생 = a soon-to-graduate student
examples: 언니는 대학을 졸업했어요.
My older sister graduated from university.
School = direct object with 를/을: 대학을 졸업했어요
저는 올해 졸업하고 싶어요.
I want to graduate this year.
~고 싶어요 expresses your own wish; 올해 = this year
학점이 모자라서 올해는 졸업 못 해요.
I'm short on credits, so I can't graduate this year.
학점 = course credits; impossible form splits as 졸업 못 해요
nuance: 졸업하다 is Sino-Korean 卒業 — 卒 'finish/complete' + 業 'studies/work' — so 'complete one's studies' and receive a diploma. Its exact opposite is 입학하다 (入學, enter a school); a softer related word is 끝나다 'to end', but a course 끝나다, whereas a person 졸업하다. The crucial English-speaker pitfall is the particle: English 'graduate FROM university' makes learners reach for 에서, but Korean treats the school as a direct OBJECT — 대학교를 졸업하다, never 대학교에서 졸업하다. As a noun+하다 verb it conjugates on 하다 (졸업해요, 졸업했어요, formal 졸업합니다), and the negative/impossible forms split the noun (졸업 안 해요, 졸업 못 해요). Note Koreans very often state it in the past about themselves — 저 작년에 졸업했어요 — because graduating is a completed life event; the present 졸업해요 usually means a scheduled near-future ('I graduate this year').

usage: the school takes 에 (entered-into), NOT 를: 대학교에 입학해요
입학 here is a noun modifying 시험; 시험을 보다 = sit an exam
to start school in the new term
새 학기 = new semester; 에 marks the time you enter
to congratulate someone on starting school
축하하다 = congratulate; 입학 축하해요! is the set phrase
examples: 동생이 중학교에 입학해요.
My younger sibling is starting middle school.
School entered = 에: 중학교에 입학해요
저는 좋은 대학에 입학하고 싶어요.
I want to get into a good university.
~고 싶어요 = want to; 좋은 대학 = a good university
성적이 낮아서 그 학교에 입학 못 해요.
My grades are low, so I can't get into that school.
Reason ~아서 + impossible form split: 입학 못 해요
nuance: 입학하다 is Sino-Korean 入學 — 入 'enter' + 學 'learning/school' — literally 'enter into learning', i.e. be admitted to and begin a school. Its exact opposite is 졸업하다 (卒業). Here is a beautiful particle trap that mirrors its opposite: 입학하다 uses 에 ('enter INTO' a school — 대학에 입학하다), whereas 졸업하다 uses 를 (대학을 졸업하다). English 'enroll IN' luckily matches the 에 here, but learners who memorized 졸업하다's 를 wrongly carry it over. Don't confuse 입학하다 with 등록하다 'to register': 입학하다 is the once-in-a-school-career act of being admitted, while 등록하다 is the recurring paperwork of signing up (for a term, a course). As a noun+하다 verb it conjugates on 하다 (입학해요, 입학했어요, formal 입학합니다); negative and impossible split the noun (입학 안 해요, 입학 못 해요). Note the pronunciation: 입학 sounds like [이팍], the ㅂ and ㅎ fusing to ㅍ.

structuredNuance.t: Be admitted to and begin a school — 'enter into learning'.

usage: to pass the exam / make the cut
what you pass takes 에: 시험에 합격해요 (NOT 시험을)
to get accepted into a university
에 again; this is 'be admitted', the result of passing entrance screening
면접 = job/admission interview; 에 marks the hurdle you clear
to wish someone success / a pass
기원하다 = pray for; 합격 기원! is what you write on a good-luck gift
examples: 시험에 합격했어요!
I passed the exam!
Use 에 for the thing passed; the past 합격했어요 reports the result
이번에는 꼭 합격하고 싶어요.
This time I really want to pass.
꼭 = for sure/without fail; 이번에는 = this time around
공부를 안 하면 합격 못 해요.
If you don't study, you can't pass.
~면 = if; impossible form splits: 합격 못 해요
nuance: 합격하다 is Sino-Korean 合格 — 合 'meet/match' + 格 'standard' — literally 'meet the standard', i.e. clear a cut-off and pass a test, interview, or admissions screen. Its opposite is 불합격하다 (不合格) or, much more colloquially, 떨어지다 'to fall/drop' (시험에 떨어졌어요 = I failed/flunked). Don't confuse 합격하다 with 통과하다 'to pass through': 통과하다 is moving past a checkpoint or a bill passing, while 합격하다 specifically means meeting a qualifying standard. The headline English-speaker pitfall is the particle: English 'pass THE exam' (object) makes learners write 시험을 합격하다, but Korean uses 에 — 시험에 합격하다 — because you're 'matching up TO the standard'. Note also 합격하다 (verb) vs 합격 (the noun, 'a pass/acceptance'): the noun is what you put on banners — 합격 축하해! As a noun+하다 verb it conjugates on 하다 (합격해요, 합격했어요, formal 합격합니다); negative/impossible split the noun (합격 안 해요, 합격 못 해요).

usage: the skill drilled takes 을/를: 발음을 연습해요
instruments and skills are objects of 연습하다; 를 marks them
열심히 = hard, with effort; the most natural adverb partner
연습 modifies 문제 (problem); 문제를 풀다 = solve problems
examples: 저는 매일 한국어를 연습해요.
I practice Korean every day.
What you drill is the object: 한국어를 연습해요
우리 같이 노래를 연습할까요?
Shall we practice the song together?
~ㄹ까요? suggests doing it together; 같이 = together
시간이 없어서 오늘은 연습 못 해요.
I have no time, so I can't practice today.
~아서 reason + impossible split: 연습 못 해요
nuance: 연습하다 is Sino-Korean 練習 — 練 'train/temper (as in tempering metal)' + 習 'repeatedly do/learn' — so 'train by repetition', i.e. drill a skill until it improves. The key contrast is with 공부하다 'to study': 공부하다 is taking in knowledge (grammar, facts, theory), whereas 연습하다 is repeated hands-on doing to build a SKILL — you 공부해 grammar but 연습해 speaking and piano. A closely related word is 훈련하다 (訓練, 'train'), which is more systematic/physical (soldiers, athletes), while 연습하다 is everyday practice. The thing practiced is a direct OBJECT with 을/를: 발음을 연습하다. The English-speaker pitfall is twofold: don't say 발음에 연습하다 (no 에), and don't reach for 공부하다 when you mean drilling a skill. As a noun+하다 verb it conjugates on 하다 (연습해요, 연습했어요, formal 연습합니다); negative/impossible split the noun (연습 안 해요, 연습 못 해요).

usage: what you commit to memory is an object with 를: 단어를 외워요
통째로 = in one whole chunk; the classic adverb for rote learning
줄줄 = fluently, in a flowing stream; 줄줄 외워요 = knows it cold
to take a test from memory
외워서 = having memorized; ~서 chains 'memorize and then…'
examples: 저는 단어를 외워요.
I memorize words.
Note the stem 외우- + 어요 contracts 우+어 → 워: 외워요
이 문장을 다 외워야 해요.
I have to memorize this whole sentence.
다 = all; obligation ~아야 해요 → 외워야 해요
단어가 너무 많아서 다 못 외워요.
There are too many words, so I can't memorize them all.
Native verb: impossible form is just 못 외워요 (no splitting)
nuance: 외우다 is a NATIVE Korean verb (no hanja), meaning to commit something to memory deliberately — to get it 'by heart' through effort. Contrast it sharply with 기억하다 (記憶, 'remember/recall'): 외우다 is the act of putting info IN ('I'll memorize these words tonight'), while 기억하다 is having or pulling it back OUT ('Do you remember my number?'). Mixing them is the #1 English-speaker error, because English 'remember' blurs both. A near-synonym 암기하다 (暗記) means the same as 외우다 but sounds more bookish/formal. Crucially, because 외우다 is native (not noun+하다), its conjugation differs from every other verb on this list: the stem 외우- meets 어요 and the 우 + 어 fuse to 워 → 외워요, past 외웠어요; the negative is the simple 안 외워요 and impossible 못 외워요 — there is NO noun to split off. Common collocations: 단어를 외우다, 통째로 외우다, 줄줄 외우다.

Because 외우다 is native (not noun+하다), its conjugation differs from every other verb on this list: the stem 외우- meets 어요 and the 우 + 어 fuse to 워 → 외워요, past 외웠어요; the negative is the simple 안 외워요 and impossible 못 외워요 — there is NO noun to split off.
Mixing 외우다 and 기억하다 is the #1 English-speaker error, because English 'remember' blurs both — putting IN vs pulling back OUT.

mistakes: Using 기억하다 where 외우다 is meant: 'I need to memorize these words' is 단어를 외워야 해요, not 기억해야 해요 (which leans toward 'recall'). 외우다 = put into memory; 기억하다 = recall from memory.
Mis-contracting the 요-form as 외우어요 or 외우요 — the 우 + 어 must fuse to 워: 외워요, past 외웠어요.
Splitting the negative like a 하다 verb (외우 안 해요) — 외우다 is one native verb, so it's simply 안 외워요 / 못 외워요.

usage: 배운 내용 = the learned content; takes 을 as the object reviewed
수업 후에 = after class; 후에 marks the time you do it
꼼꼼하게 = meticulously; natural adverb for careful review
the standard paired phrase contrasting after-study and before-study
examples: 저는 자기 전에 복습해요.
I review before going to bed.
자기 전에 = before sleeping; ~기 전에 = before doing
시험 전에 같이 복습할까요?
Shall we review together before the exam?
~ㄹ까요? proposes; 같이 = together
너무 졸려서 오늘은 복습 못 해요.
I'm too sleepy to review today.
~아서 reason + impossible split: 복습 못 해요
nuance: 복습하다 is Sino-Korean 復習 — 復 'again/repeat' + 習 'study' — literally 'study again', i.e. go back over material you've already learned to lock it in. Its mirror-image partner is 예습하다 (豫習, 豫 'in advance' + 習 'study'), meaning to study a lesson BEFORE class; Koreans habitually pair them as 예습과 복습. Don't confuse 복습하다 with 연습하다 (練習): both end in 습(習), but 복습하다 is re-studying KNOWLEDGE you covered, while 연습하다 is drilling a SKILL by repetition — you 복습해 yesterday's grammar but 연습해 your pronunciation. Note the 復 here is read 복 (not 부 as in 부활); the whole word is pronounced [복씁하다] with a tensed ㅆ. As a noun+하다 verb it conjugates entirely on 하다 (복습해요, 복습했어요, formal 복습합니다); the negative and impossible forms split the noun (복습 안 해요, 복습 못 해요), never 안 복습해요.

usage: 결과 = results; what you make public takes 을/를
to give a presentation in class
in this 'do a presentation' sense, the place takes 에서: 수업에서 발표해요
발표 modifies 자료 (materials); 자료를 만들다 = prepare materials
합격자 = those who passed; the 'officially make public' sense
examples: 내일 수업에서 제가 발표해요.
I'm presenting in class tomorrow.
Doing a presentation IN a place = 에서: 수업에서 발표해요
이 자료를 같이 발표할까요?
Shall we present this material together?
~ㄹ까요? proposes; 자료 = the material shown
너무 긴장해서 발표 못 해요.
I'm so nervous I can't present.
긴장하다 = be nervous; impossible split: 발표 못 해요
nuance: 발표하다 is Sino-Korean 發表 — 發 'issue/emit' + 表 'express/show outwardly' — so 'issue something into the open'. It has two senses: (1) give a presentation/talk in front of an audience (수업에서 발표하다), and (2) officially announce/release information (정부가 결과를 발표하다 — the government announced the results). Contrast it with 설명하다 (說明, 'explain'): 설명하다 is clarifying so someone understands a point, while 발표하다 is the public act of presenting or announcing as a whole. Also distinguish 발표하다 from 말하다 'to say' — 발표하다 implies prepared, formal, to-an-audience delivery. A particle nuance: in the 'present' sense the location uses 에서 (수업에서), but the content shown is an object (자료를 발표하다). As a noun+하다 verb it conjugates on 하다 (발표해요, 발표했어요, formal 발표합니다); negative/impossible split the noun (발표 안 해요, 발표 못 해요).

usage: 서류 = documents/papers; the thing handed in takes 을/를
보고서 = report; the classic workplace collocation
기한 안에 = within the deadline; 안에 = inside (a time limit)
to prepare the documents to be submitted
제출 modifies 서류; 준비하다 = get ready
examples: 오늘까지 숙제를 제출해야 해요.
I have to hand in the homework by today.
오늘까지 = by today (deadline with 까지); obligation 제출해야 해요
이 신청서를 여기에 제출해 주세요.
Please submit this application here.
여기에 = to here; ~아 주세요 = please do (for me)
서류가 부족해서 지금 제출 못 해요.
I'm missing documents, so I can't submit now.
부족하다 = be lacking; impossible split: 제출 못 해요
nuance: 제출하다 is Sino-Korean 提出 — 提 'lift/raise up' + 出 'out' — so 'put forward, hand out', i.e. formally submit a document, application, or assignment to an authority. Its register is the key point: 제출하다 is the formal, official word, while everyday speech often just uses 내다 'to put out/hand in' — students say 숙제를 냈어요 casually but write 과제를 제출했습니다 formally. The opposite side of the transaction is 받다 'to receive'/접수하다 'to accept (a submission)'. The English-speaker pitfall: 'submit TO the office' tempts an English-style structure, but the destination simply takes 에 (사무실에 제출하다) and the document is a direct object (서류를 제출하다). As a noun+하다 verb it conjugates on 하다 (제출해요, 제출했어요, formal 제출합니다); negative/impossible split the noun (제출 안 해요, 제출 못 해요). Note pronunciation [제출하다] is straightforward, but watch the polite request form 제출해 주세요.

usage: the event takes 에 (NOT 를): 회의에 참석해요
ceremonies are classic partners; 에 marks the event joined
꼭 = for sure; 꼭 참석해 주세요 = please be sure to come (formal invite)
to let (someone) know whether you'll attend
examples: 내일 회의에 참석해야 해요.
I have to attend the meeting tomorrow.
Event attended = 에: 회의에 참석해요 (never 회의를)
이번 모임에 같이 참석할까요?
Shall we attend this gathering together?
모임 = get-together; ~ㄹ까요? proposes going together
일정이 겹쳐서 행사에 참석 못 해요.
My schedule clashes, so I can't attend the event.
겹치다 = overlap; impossible split: 참석 못 해요
nuance: 참석하다 is Sino-Korean 參席 — 參 'take part' + 席 'seat' — literally 'take one's seat (and take part)', i.e. attend a formal event like a meeting, ceremony, or banquet. Its register is more formal than just 가다 'to go'; you 결혼식에 가요 casually but 결혼식에 참석합니다 in polite/written contexts. Distinguish it from its close cousin 참가하다 (參加, 'participate/enter'): 참석하다 emphasizes being PRESENT and seated at a gathering, while 참가하다 emphasizes actively TAKING PART (참가하다 fits a contest, race, or program — 대회에 참가하다). The big English-speaker pitfall is the particle: English 'attend THE meeting' (object) drives learners to 회의를 참석하다, but Korean uses 에 — 회의에 참석하다 — because you 'join INTO' the event. As a noun+하다 verb it conjugates on 하다 (참석해요, 참석했어요, formal 참석합니다); negative/impossible split the noun (참석 안 해요, 참석 못 해요).

usage: to get a job at a company
the employer takes 에: 회사에 취직해요 (NOT 회사를)
to land a job at a big conglomerate
대기업 = large corporation; the aspirational collocation
to prepare for getting a job (job-hunt)
취직 준비 = job-search prep; overlaps with 취업 준비
잘 되다 = to go well; 요즘 취직이 잘 안 돼요 = jobs are hard to get these days
examples: 저는 큰 회사에 취직하고 싶어요.
I want to get a job at a big company.
Employer = 에: 회사에 취직하다; ~고 싶어요 = want to
형은 작년에 병원에 취직했어요.
My older brother got a job at a hospital last year.
Completed event → past 취직했어요; 병원에 = at a hospital
경력이 없어서 아직 취직 못 해요.
I have no experience, so I can't get a job yet.
경력 = work experience; impossible split: 취직 못 해요
nuance: 취직하다 is Sino-Korean 就職 — 就 'take up/settle into' + 職 'a post/position' — literally 'take up a post', i.e. get hired and start a job. It nearly overlaps with 취업하다 (就業, 'take up work'): in daily speech they're interchangeable, but 취직 leans toward landing a specific job/post at a company, while 취업 is the broader 'entering employment' (you'll see 취업률 'employment rate', 취업 준비생 'job seeker'). Don't confuse 취직하다 with 일하다 'to work': 취직하다 is the one-time event of GETTING the job, while 일하다 is the ongoing doing of work — 좋은 데 취직해서 열심히 일해요 (I got a good job and work hard). The English-speaker pitfall is the particle: 'get a job AT a company' makes learners write 회사를 취직하다, but the employer takes 에 — 회사에 취직하다. As a noun+하다 verb it conjugates on 하다 (취직해요, 취직했어요, formal 취직합니다); negative/impossible split the noun (취직 안 해요, 취직 못 해요).
